title: Tata's iPhone Parts Factory Faces Shutdown Threat After Regulators Find Contaminated Farmland Water.
excerpt: Tamil Nadu's pollution board says wastewater from Tata Electronics' Hosur plant overflowed into nearby agricultural wells. Tata says its own tests show full compliance.
body:
India's pollution regulator has alleged that wastewater from a Tata Electronics factory — one that makes back panels and other components for Apple's iPhone — has contaminated groundwater feeding nearby farmland. The Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board has warned of a forced shutdown unless Tata provides a satisfactory explanation.

The allegation, detailed in a previously unreported regulatory notice dated May 25 and reviewed by Reuters, strikes at the heart of India's ambitions to become the world's second-largest iPhone manufacturing base.

## Five Inspections, No Corrective Action

Farmers near the Tata plant in Hosur, a town in southern Tamil Nadu, had been complaining for months that wastewater from the factory was seeping into their land and open wells. Those complaints triggered five state inspections between December 2025 and May 2026.

The inspections found that Tata discharged wastewater into a rainwater harvesting pond inside the facility. That pond overflowed, and the contamination spread to "groundwater in the open wells located in the adjacent agricultural lands," according to the pollution board's notice.

More damning: the board says Tata had not taken any corrective action on instructions issued in a previous letter dated December 23, 2025 — meaning the company was warned nearly six months ago and allegedly did nothing.

The May notice asked Tata to explain why power to the unit should not be cut and the facility shuttered for violating environmental rules.

## Tata Pushes Back

Tata Electronics told Reuters it had commissioned an independent analysis through an accredited laboratory, and that the study determined the company was "in full compliance with all regulatory norms." The company said it was "committed to responsible business practices and protection of the environment and local communities" and had responded to the pollution authorities, though it gave no further details.

Apple, which maintains strict rules on how its suppliers handle wastewater, did not respond to Reuters' request for comment. Nor did the Tamil Nadu state government.

## A Pattern of Supply Chain Trouble

The Hosur contamination notice is not an isolated incident. Apple's India supply chain has been dogged by a series of problems over the past three years:

A fire at Tata's Hosur plant in September 2024 briefly halted iPhone component production. A separate fire at former supplier Pegatron's iPhone plant in September 2023 shut production for days. In 2024, a Reuters investigation found that Foxconn — Apple's largest Indian contractor — had systematically excluded married women from assembly jobs at one of its plants.

India's environment ministry told parliament in February that 4.4 per cent of the country's 544,364 industrial units had been found non-compliant with environmental standards over the past five years. More than 3,600 facilities were shut down by pollution control departments in that period.

## The Stakes for India's Manufacturing Push

India is projected to make 26 per cent of all iPhones globally in 2026, up from just 6 per cent four years ago, according to Counterpoint Research. The country now hosts five iPhone factories between Tata and Foxconn, with a new $2.6 billion Foxconn plant near Bengaluru scaling up operations.

Tata has moved aggressively to become Apple's anchor Indian partner. It acquired Wistron's iPhone assembly plant in Karnataka, took a majority stake in Pegatron's only Indian iPhone factory, and is building what is intended to be the country's largest iPhone assembly plant — also in Tamil Nadu — with capacity for 20 assembly lines and 50,000 workers.

But scale without environmental governance creates its own risks. A forced shutdown at Hosur, even temporarily, would disrupt Apple's carefully orchestrated production diversification away from China. And for the farmers whose wells are allegedly contaminated, the costs of India's manufacturing ambitions are measured not in units shipped but in water they can no longer drink.

India's environment ministry data tells a broader story: the country's rapid industrialisation is running ahead of its regulatory capacity. For every factory that gets shut down, dozens more operate in grey zones where compliance is aspirational rather than enforced. The Tata case is significant precisely because the company involved is not some obscure operator — it is one of India's most storied conglomerates, making products for the world's most valuable company.
